description: Coyolxauhqui is a significant figure in Aztec mythology, primarily known as the goddess of the moon. Her story is intertwined with the birth of Huitzilopochtli, the Aztec god of war and sun. According to the myth, Coyolxauhqui, along with her 400 brothers (the Centzon Huitznahua), plotted to kill their mother, Coatlicue, who had become pregnant in a miraculous manner. However, Huitzilopochtli was born fully armed and immediately slew Coyolxauhqui, dismembering her body and scattering the pieces on the mountain Coatepec. This act established Huitzilopochtli's dominance and solidified the Aztec's belief in the cyclical nature of life, death, and rebirth. The dismemberment of Coyolxauhqui is believed to be represented by the large stone disc found at the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlan, depicting the goddess in a fragmented state.

extendedContent.title: Origins & Mythology
extendedContent.content: Coyolxauhqui's origin lies in the foundational myth of Huitzilopochtli's birth. Coatlicue, while sweeping, was impregnated by a ball of feathers. This angered Coyolxauhqui and her brothers, the Centzon Huitznahua, who considered it a dishonorable pregnancy. They decided to kill Coatlicue, but Huitzilopochtli was born fully armed and defended his mother, slaying Coyolxauhqui and scattering her limbs across the mountain. This event is central to Aztec cosmology, representing the daily victory of the sun (Huitzilopochtli) over the moon (Coyolxauhqui) and the stars (Centzon Huitznahua).

extendedContent.title: Role & Significance
extendedContent.content: Coyolxauhqui's role in Aztec mythology is multifaceted. She represents the moon, and her defeat symbolizes the sun's dominance over the night. Her dismemberment is a powerful image that reflects the cyclical nature of time and the constant struggle between opposing forces. The Coyolxauhqui Stone, discovered at the Templo Mayor, served as a sacrificial platform, reinforcing the idea that sacrifice was necessary to maintain cosmic order. Her story also served as a cautionary tale against rebellion and the disruption of social hierarchies. The goddess also embodied female anger and resistance within the Aztec pantheon.

extendedContent.title: Symbolism & Interpretation
extendedContent.content: Coyolxauhqui's symbolism is deeply rooted in lunar cycles and the feminine principle. Her dismemberment symbolizes the waning moon, while Huitzilopochtli's victory represents the sun's strength. The scattering of her limbs across the mountain Coatepec can be interpreted as the distribution of lunar energy across the landscape. Some scholars suggest that Coyolxauhqui represents the forces of chaos and disorder, which must be overcome by the forces of order and civilization. The Coyolxauhqui Stone, with its detailed depiction of the dismembered goddess, serves as a powerful reminder of the consequences of challenging the established order.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: Coyolxauhqui's legacy continues to resonate in modern Mexican culture and art. The discovery of the Coyolxauhqui Stone in 1978 was a significant event that sparked renewed interest in Aztec history and mythology. Her image has become a symbol of indigenous resistance and female empowerment. Artists and writers continue to draw inspiration from her story, exploring themes of rebellion, sacrifice, and the cyclical nature of life. The goddess appears in various forms of popular culture, including literature, film, and visual arts, ensuring that her story continues to be told and reinterpreted for new generations.
